solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Fine south coast resort out of bounds?

indicators.note: with its bounds gone, the resort's name loses its first and last letters

parts.note: Brighton is a seaside resort on England's south coast

explanation.surface: A query about whether a fine seaside town on the south coast is off limits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of bounds' strips the outer letters B and N from BRIGHTON.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are casual expressions of agreement, as in replying 'OK' to a suggestion.

clue.text: Read about big cat leaping over son

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: the rearranged cat goes over, that is round, the letter for son
leaping means the cat's letters jump into a new arrangement

parts.note: a tiger is a big cat

explanation.surface: Reading about a tiger jumping over a boy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaping' rearranges TIGER to GITER, which 'over' wraps round S.
explanation.definitionFit: A meter or gauge that shows a reading is said to record or display that figure.

clue.text: Waste from gulls usually, also numerous other sources

indicators.note: sources are where things begin, so the first letter of each word is taken

explanation.surface: Droppings come mostly from seabirds, and from plenty of others too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sources' picks the first letter of each of five words.
explanation.definitionFit: Accumulated seabird droppings are a natural waste product, used as fertiliser.

clue.text: Tax lovelorn politician

indicators.note: lorn means bereft, so the word is without love, the O of a zero score in tennis

parts.note: a Tory is a member of the UK Conservative Party

explanation.surface: A tax-collecting Conservative pining for love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax' is a verb: to strain or test. Love is O as nil in tennis.
explanation.definitionFit: To tax someone's patience is to strain or test it, as in sorely trying it.

clue.text: Ecstasy bachelor extracted from plant

indicators.note: taken out of, so one letter is removed from the plant's name

parts.note: euphorbia is the spurge genus of plants

explanation.surface: The drug ecstasy obtained by a single man from a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ecstasy' looks like the drug, but it is simply the feeling. 'extracted from' takes the B out of EUPHORBIA, the spurge plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecstasy and this word both name an intense state of happiness and elation.

clue.text: Straighten out a foreign lad wanting more

parts.note: un is French for a
Oliver Twist is the Dickens orphan who asks for more gruel

explanation.surface: Sort out a foreign boy who keeps asking for more.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist famously asks 'Please, sir, I want some more' in the Dickens novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Undoing a coil or curl leaves something straight again.

clue.text: Suspended sport's execution, seizing golf hat

indicators.note: grabbing hold of, so the execution word takes the other letters inside

parts.note: hanging is a method of execution
Golf is the radio alphabet word for G
lid is slang for a hat

explanation.surface: A sport's carrying out, grabbing a golfing cap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'execution' looks like performance but is a method of putting to death; 'seizing' means the golf letter and the hat go inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Flying from a kite-like wing with the pilot hanging below is an airborne sport.

clue.text: Communist and German colonist no longer needed

parts.note: red is a common label for a communist
und is German for and
an ant lives in a colony

explanation.surface: A Communist and a German settler are now surplus to requirements.
explanation.definitionFit: Workers laid off as surplus to requirements are described as superfluous to need.

clue.text: British sport fitting screens without warning

indicators.note: conceals behind it, so the word for fitting surrounds the other letters

parts.note: apt means suitable or fitting
RU stands for Rugby Union

explanation.surface: A British sport's fixture suddenly blocking out the view.
explanation.walkthrough: 'screens' means hides, so the word for fitting goes around British and the rugby code.
explanation.definitionFit: Something sudden and unexpected happens without any warning.

clue.text: Big Smoke firm acting to stop gunmen

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company

indicators.note: plugging a gap, so the word for acting goes inside the gunmen

parts.note: RA is the Royal Artillery, the gunners
on, as an actor is on stage

explanation.surface: A London company performing to halt armed men.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big Smoke' suggests London, but it is a large cigar.
explanation.definitionFit: A long, straight-sided cigar is a big thing to smoke.

clue.text: Vessel in service yielding easy money with craft

parts.note: gravy is slang for money or profit gained with little effort
a craft is a boat

explanation.surface: A ship in naval service earning easy money from its trade.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'service' is a dinner service, a set of tableware, not military duty.
explanation.definitionFit: A jug-like vessel for pouring sauce is one piece of a matching set of tableware.

clue.text: Northern Irish accepting a donation, originally for the pits

indicators.note: taking in, so the letters for Northern Irish hold what follows

parts.note: N for northern and IR for Irish, both standard abbreviations

indicators.note: originally means the first letter of donation is used

explanation.surface: A Northern Irish charity drive taking a gift intended for coal mines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the pits' reads as coal mines but means the worst possible point.
explanation.definitionFit: The lowest point of fortunes is the worst place to be, which is what 'the pits' describes colloquially.

clue.text: Weakness of Ernie Wise, say, mostly no good

indicators.note: mostly means the last letter of the phrase is dropped

parts.note: Ernie Wise, the smaller half of the British double act Morecambe and Wise, is an example of a short comic

explanation.surface: A jibe at comedian Ernie Wise's failing, being mostly not much good.
explanation.walkthrough: Ernie Wise was the short partner in the famous British comedy duo Morecambe and Wise; 'say' marks him as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: A failing or defect is a weakness in a person or plan.

clue.text: Flipping game having had too many knowing signals

parts.note: tiddly is British slang for slightly drunk
winks are knowing signals to someone

explanation.surface: A drunk player giving sly signals over a game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' sounds like a mild curse but describes the counters being flipped.
explanation.definitionFit: Players flick small discs into a cup, flipping them across the table in this game.

clue.text: Pinch St Andrews flag back

indicators.note: back means the word for the flag is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: St Andrews is a famous golf course, and the flagstick on a golf green is called the pin

explanation.surface: Steal the Scottish saltire flag back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'St Andrews flag' suggests the Scottish saltire, but it is the flagstick on a golf green at St Andrews.
explanation.definitionFit: To pinch is to squeeze between finger and thumb, and also to take a quick small amount.

clue.text: Oz native's daughter visiting European country

indicators.note: a visitor goes inside, so the letter for daughter sits within the other letters

parts.note: China is a country

explanation.surface: An Australian's daughter on a trip to a European country.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz is Australia; the D goes inside E CHINA, after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiny anteater is a mammal found in Australia, so it is native to Oz.

clue.text: Cry from magicians showing ropes they tangled

indicators.note: knotted up, so the letters are mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: Conjurors' trick of displaying ropes they knotted.
explanation.definitionFit: A conjuror exclaims this at the moment a trick is revealed.

clue.text: Island's top-class whiskey consumed in function

indicators.note: swallowed by, so these letters go inside the function

parts.note: tan, short for tangent, is a trigonometric function
A1 means first-rate, read as AI
Whiskey is the radio alphabet word for W

explanation.surface: An island's best whiskey being drunk at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'function' looks like a party but is the trigonometric tangent; A1 is written AI.
explanation.definitionFit: The country formerly known as Formosa is a large island off the Chinese coast.

clue.text: Genuine duck is dearest

parts.note: true means genuine or real
a duck in cricket is a score of nothing, and love means nil in tennis

explanation.surface: A real duck is the most precious thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'duck' looks like the bird or a term of endearment but is zero.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweetheart is one's dearest, the person one loves most.

clue.text: US city wife follows extra rule

indicators.note: follows means the city and wife come after the extra

parts.note: in cricket a bye is an extra, a run not scored off the bat
LA is Los Angeles

explanation.surface: An additional regulation laid down by a wife in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: A bye in cricket is a run conceded without the ball touching the bat, counted as an extra.
explanation.definitionFit: A local regulation made by a council or company is a kind of rule.

clue.text: West Indies action man eats with former husband

indicators.note: takes in, so the action man swallows the letter

parts.note: a doer is a person of action

explanation.surface: A Caribbean man of action dining with his ex.
explanation.walkthrough: A wife's death makes her husband 'former', the clue's twist on ex.
explanation.definitionFit: A man whose wife has died is no longer a husband.

clue.text: 14 guides go back to collect paper

indicators.note: the reversed guides gather the paper inside them
go back means the word for the guides is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: reins are what a rider steers a horse with
FT is the Financial Times newspaper

explanation.surface: Tour guides return to pick up a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: '14' points to the answer at 14 across, a small drink. 'go back' reverses the guides, and 'to collect' wraps them round the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A short tot of spirits is a small drink, just as the cross-referenced answer is.

clue.text: Tetchy teacher extremely touchy about height

indicators.note: round, so the teacher's word goes around the letter for height

parts.note: sir is how pupils address a male teacher

indicators.note: extremely means the first and last letters of touchy are used

explanation.surface: An irritable teacher very sensitive about his height.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts SIR round H.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words mean irritable and quick to take offence; the answer is British slang.

clue.text: Account of old soldiers receiving Prince Harry

indicators.note: taking in, so the soldiers' letters hold the prince's name

parts.note: the BEF was the British Expeditionary Force of the world wars
Prince Hal is Shakespeare's name for the young Henry V

explanation.surface: A story of veterans welcoming Prince Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prince Harry' suggests the modern royal, but it is Shakespeare's Hal.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting on someone's account and acting on their part mean the same: for their sake.

clue.text: Royal couple stray

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, is the Queen's royal cipher
the queen's partner in the pair is a king, R for Rex

explanation.surface: A king and queen wander off.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal pair is read as ER (Elizabeth Regina, the Queen) joined by R (Rex, a king).
explanation.definitionFit: To go astray morally or from the right path is to make a mistake.

clue.text: We'd decking rebuilt with a centrepiece at reception?

indicators.note: the letters are put together again in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Our deck reconstructed with an ornamental feature at a party venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rebuilt' rearranges WEDDECKING and A; the 'reception' is a marriage party, and the question mark flags the definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: The tiered confection is the showpiece at a marriage reception, an example of a centrepiece.

clue.text: A sprinkler and its target, perhaps, appeared

parts.note: a rose is the perforated nozzle of a watering can, and a rose bush is what it might water

explanation.surface: A garden sprinkler and the plant it waters.
explanation.walkthrough: One word names both the spray head on a watering can and the flower it waters.
explanation.definitionFit: To come up or emerge into view is to appear, as the sun did at dawn.

clue.text: A Republican lad's crime

parts.note: a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A Republican's son committing an offence.
explanation.definitionFit: Deliberately setting fire to property is a criminal offence.

clue.text: Endless battle cramps potty game

indicators.note: confines, so the battle's letters enclose the pot
endless means the battle's name loses its final letter

parts.note: Waterloo was the 1815 battle
a po is a chamber pot

explanation.surface: A never-ending battle restricts a silly game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'potty' looks like 'crazy' but is a chamber pot, PO. 'Endless' cuts WATERLOO to WATERLO.
explanation.definitionFit: A team sport played in a swimming pool is a game.

clue.text: Upended Beetle's axle

indicators.note: turned upside down, which in a down entry reads the word backwards

parts.note: a dor is a dung beetle

explanation.surface: A capsized VW Beetle's axle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beetle' hints at the Volkswagen car, but it is the insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A rod is a straight bar, of which an axle is one example.

clue.text: Maybe needing plaster, pays deposit

parts.note: to foot a bill is to pay it
ore is a mineral deposit

explanation.surface: Someone who may need a cast hands over a down payment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plaster' suggests a cast for a broken limb, but here it is a sticking plaster for blisters.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with aching, blistered feet after walking might well want a sticking plaster.

clue.text: Bond had failed previously once

indicators.note: failed means the letters of had broke down and are rearranged

parts.note: ere is an old-fashioned word for before

explanation.surface: A James Bond mission that once went wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bond' looks like the spy but is a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To bond is to stick, as glue joins two surfaces.
